aspects.says: A builder's name(prefix, start) names each thread it makes, counting up from start.
Carrier threads come from a dedicated ForkJoinPool whose size defaults to the processor count, separate from the common pool.
aspects.reason: a scheduler setting that a graded test cannot observe reliably (which carrier runs a virtual thread is up to the scheduler); the quiz's unmount question covers what a carrier is for

aspects.says: A virtual thread's stack starts at a few hundred bytes and grows on demand, which makes one far cheaper to create than a platform thread.
aspects.reason: a cost and memory claim that no test can measure deterministically on a shared runner; the fanout practice keeps twenty virtual threads in flight at once, which is the use this cheapness allows

aspects.says: Virtual threads bring no gain for CPU-bound work, which never reaches a blocking point to unmount at; a fixed platform pool sized to the cores suits it.
Thread.currentThread() inside a virtual thread returns the virtual thread, not its carrier.
aspects.reason: a minor fact with nothing to write; the fanout test reads Thread.currentThread().isVirtual() inside each fetch and relies on it

aspects.says: Virtual threads are daemon threads, so work started on them must be waited for or the program may end first.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: Virtual threads are always daemon and always NORM_PRIORITY: setDaemon(false) throws and setPriority is ignored.
aspects.reason: practised on the sibling page 6.7.2 by its traits practice, which chooses a platform thread when a spec needs a non-daemon thread or a priority

aspects.says: An interrupted virtual thread blocked in sleep or take throws InterruptedException at once, and the handler restores the interrupt status instead of swallowing it.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: A thread that may never finish is joined with a timeout, so the caller is never blocked forever.
Virtual threads previewed in Java 19 and 20 and became final in Java 21 (JEP 444).
aspects.reason: version history, an incidental detail with nothing to practise

aspects.says: A virtual thread is mounted on a carrier thread only while it runs and unmounts at a blocking call, freeing the carrier for other virtual threads.
basis: section:6.7.1.1. Overview of Project Loom and Virtual Threads

aspects.says: Virtual threads are not pooled: a fixed pool of them caps concurrency exactly like a pool of platform threads.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() starts a new virtual thread for every task, and closing it in try-with-resources waits for all of them.
ScopedValue, a preview API in Java 21, is a lighter alternative to ThreadLocal for many virtual threads.
aspects.reason: a preview API in Java 21 that the practice build does not enable (no --enable-preview), so no graded code can use it; the context practice teaches the ThreadLocal clean-up that ScopedValue makes automatic

aspects.says: A Semaphore, not a smaller pool, limits how many virtual threads use a scarce resource at once, with the permit released in finally.
Structured concurrency, a preview API in Java 21, treats a group of related virtual-thread tasks as one unit for errors and cancellation.
aspects.reason: a preview API in Java 21 that the practice build does not enable, so no graded code can use it; the page itself only names it as a future direction

aspects.says: Each virtual thread has its own ThreadLocal value, and the value is removed in finally when the work ends.
Virtual threads raise throughput by keeping more tasks in flight; they do not make a single task faster.
Thread.ofVirtual() and Thread.startVirtualThread() create virtual threads, and isVirtual() tells a virtual thread from a platform one.
basis: section:6.7.1.2. Creating and Managing Virtual Threads
